messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Rajesh

Rajesh was forty-nine when his wife found him standing in the kitchen at three in the morning, still in his work uniform, unable to explain why he couldn't sleep. He had been a military medic for twenty-three years—steady, competent, the kind of man who could stabilize a casualty in chaos and move on. But that steadiness had fractured eight months ago, during the six weeks he had spent with Marcus, a man he had met at a veterans' support group and had allowed into his home after his marriage had grown distant. Marcus had seemed to understand the weight of service in ways his wife could not. What Rajesh had not understood was that Marcus carried his own violence like a weapon, and that it would be turned on him with shocking brutality.

The assault had happened on a Tuesday evening. Marcus had been drinking, and Rajesh had suggested he leave. The refusal had escalated into a confrontation—fists, a thrown lamp, Rajesh's head against the doorframe, ribs struck so hard he thought one had cracked. What stayed with him most was not the pain itself, but the smell: Marcus's sweat, acrid and close, the animal reek of aggression that had filled his nostrils as he lay on the kitchen tile trying to protect his face. When it ended, Rajesh had called the police. Marcus had been arrested, but the case had stalled in the system, and no conviction had come. The man responsible walked free. That fact, more than the bruises, had begun to poison everything.

In the weeks after, Rajesh had noticed how certain things would trigger the memory to return unbidden. When he encountered a police officer in uniform at the grocery store, the sight of the badge would jolt him, and suddenly he was back on the kitchen floor, the memory so vivid and immediate that he felt the pain blooming again in his ribs and across his jaw as if the fists were still landing. When his brother-in-law visited, the presence of a known person in his space would send his nervous system into high alert, flooding him with the conviction that something terrible was about to happen—and with it came the intrusive memory, the sensation of being trapped and helpless. Worst of all was the smell of sweat. At the military base where he worked, in the gym or the barracks, the scent of human perspiration would hit him like a physical blow, and he would find himself gasping, certain he was about to be attacked again.

These triggers had begun to reshape his life in ways he could not fully control. He had started avoiding the gym entirely, despite the fact that physical fitness had been part of his identity for decades. He stopped wearing the gray athletic shirts he had owned for years, unable to tolerate the sight of them in his closet—they were too similar to what Marcus had worn that night. More broadly, he had begun avoiding other people. He declined invitations from colleagues, made excuses to his wife, and spent his off-duty hours alone in his bedroom with the door locked. The isolation felt necessary, a way of controlling which triggers he would encounter, but it had begun to corrode his marriage. His wife had stopped asking him to join her for dinners with friends. She had stopped trying to talk to him at all.

But the avoidance had not brought relief. Instead, it had deepened his sense that something fundamental had broken inside him. He had come to believe that there was something defective about him as a person—that a whole man would not be this afraid, would not be this damaged. The fact that Marcus had faced no real consequences, that the man was still out there, reinforced a darker conviction: that the world was indifferent to his suffering, that nothing in his life held meaning anymore. His work as a medic, which had once felt like a calling, now felt hollow. He went through the motions, but the purpose had drained away. This growing sense of meaninglessness and shame had paradoxically driven him deeper into avoidance. If nothing mattered, why risk encountering people or situations that might trigger the memory? Why expose himself to the physical pain that came with reliving the assault?

His hypervigilance had intensified in response. He could not fall asleep until well after midnight, lying rigid in bed, needing to stay alert in case Marcus somehow found him, even though the rational part of him knew this was unlikely. He would startle violently at ordinary sounds—a door closing, a car horn in the street—his body reacting as though the threat were immediate. He had come to feel safe only in his locked bedroom, a shrinking island of control in a world that felt fundamentally dangerous. The memory itself had become increasingly difficult to articulate. When he tried to describe what had happened to his wife or to himself, the words would not come. The event existed in his mind as a visceral, nonverbal thing—a storm of sensation and emotion that could not be translated into language, only endured.

It was his wife who finally insisted he seek help. She had found him one morning sitting on the edge of the bed, unable to get up, the weight of meaninglessness so heavy that he could not imagine a reason to move. He had come to his first appointment carrying a silence that seemed to surround him like a shield, afraid that speaking about what had happened would make it real in a way he could not survive, yet knowing that the path he was on—the avoidance, the isolation, the sleepless nights, the conviction that he was fundamentally broken—was destroying what little remained of his life.
